rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a red-tailed hawk, a compilation of measurements puts you at about 17 cycles a degree, where a human reads about 30 on an eye chart. A black kite in that compilation reads about 35, and the eagle Aquila audax up to 140. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a bald eagle, an osprey or most other species in your group.
rows.note: Rounded 33 to 35 and 138 to 140. Left out the 160 book figure (R13) because it names no species, and left out interreceptor_deg because no record has it.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: A light flashing 80 times a second looks steady to a human, who stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second. If you are a peregrine falcon, you see flicker at 125 flashes a second at least, if you are a saker falcon, at 100, and if you are a Harris's hawk, at 80. If you are a kestrel or another falcon of the genus Falco, you very likely see flicker at a fast rate like your relatives the peregrine and the saker, and for any other hawk, eagle or kite nobody has measured it.
rows.note: Peregrine figure is a lower bound ("at least 129"), so I rounded down to 125. No numbers given for carried falcons.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: Straight ahead, your two eyes look at the same patch of the world, and in the birds measured that patch is about 35 degrees wide in the red-tailed hawk, American kestrel and Cooper's hawk, 40 in the bald eagle, and 45 in the crested caracara. Behind your head the red-tailed hawk has a blind area of about 80 degrees and Cooper's hawk one of about 60. For most hawks, eagles and falcons, nobody has measured how wide the whole field is, and for many nobody has measured the overlap either.
rows.note: Left out total field widths (278 and 300 degrees): their quotes give only the blind areas, not those values.
